tldr: This paper achieves the world's first stable, closed-loop bipedal locomotion on the low-cost Poppy humanoid—a robot with few sensors and an extremely low control rate of 5 Hz—by learning linear dynamics and a fall-penalizing quadratic cost function from real-robot data using LQR.
hero_caption: The Poppy Humanoid and the four experimental locations used in the study. To prevent damage from falls, a custom suspension rig made from a clothes rack and camera straps was used; a trial was counted as a successful walk only when the straps remained slack without human intervention throughout the motion.
overview:
The Poppy Humanoid is an open-source, low-cost robot for education and research. While its 3D-printed body is lightweight, it poses severe hardware constraints for bipedal locomotion. It supports only position control with command rates at or below 5 Hz, has small feet with just 1 DOF at each ankle, and lacks an IMU or foot pressure sensors. As a result, previous research required researchers to hold its hands for support or heavily modify the hardware into a different robot.

This study tackles autonomous walking on standard, unmodified Poppy hardware without human assistance. The authors focused on failure data from open-loop trajectory playback. They designed a nominal walking trajectory with manual tuning, added small noise, and ran it on the real robot to collect 125 trials. From this dataset, they identified local linear dynamics around the nominal trajectory using least-squares system identification. Then, they formulated the condition that trajectories leading to falls should incur higher costs as a convex optimization problem (a semidefinite program) to learn a cost function for an LQR controller.

Through large-scale empirical validation on the physical robot (100 trials each in an office environment, and 80 trials each in an unseen lab environment), the closed-loop controller demonstrated statistically significant improvements ($p < 0.01$) in steps taken before falling and overall completion rates compared to open-loop playback. This work is a milestone showing that data-driven control-theoretic approaches can succeed even under extremely constrained, low-spec hardware conditions.
contributions: Demonstrated the first unassisted, closed-loop autonomous bipedal walking on the standard Poppy Humanoid despite severely limited sensors and control rates

Proposed a framework using convex optimization (semidefinite programming) to learn an LQR cost function from open-loop real-robot data, assigning higher costs to falling trials while keeping states near the nominal trajectory
Conducted extensive real-robot walking experiments totaling 360 trials across two different floor environments, showing statistically significant improvements over open-loop control
Fully open-sourced the collected walking dataset and controller code to ensure reproducibility

sections.heading: Why Has Autonomous Walking on Standard Poppy Been Impossible Until Now?
sections.summary: While the Poppy Humanoid is low-cost and extensible, autonomous walking has been hindered by its lack of sensors and low control frequency. This paper presents the first demonstration of autonomous bipedal walking on standard hardware using closed-loop LQR control with dynamics and a cost function learned from open-loop data.
sections.details:
The Poppy Humanoid is an open-source child-sized robot developed about 13 years ago for education and research. Excluding electronics and motors, its entire body is 3D-printed, making it lightweight, affordable, and easy to modify. However, attempting bipedal locomotion on the stock hardware presents formidable challenges:

- It operates strictly via position control with an extremely low reliable command rate (well below 100 Hz)
- The foot contact area is small and each ankle has only a single axis of rotation, leading to immediate underactuation if flat ground contact is lost
- Neither foot pressure sensors nor an IMU are included in the standard build, making state estimation very difficult

Consequently, past studies either had a human guide the robot by holding its hands or modified the platform substantially into a different machine. Yet, achieving reliable walking on the low-cost standard platform would provide a major stepping stone for robotics research under resource-constrained conditions.

To address this, the authors proposed combining optimal control (LQR) with machine learning. They estimated local linear dynamics around a nominal trajectory from pre-collected open-loop playback data, and then used convex optimization to learn a quadratic cost function that penalizes deviations leading to falls. This approach improved walking performance with statistical significance without altering the hardware in any way.

captions.F1: The physical Poppy robot and the four experimental locations used in the study. A safety rig combining a clothes rack and camera straps prevented fall damage; only runs where the straps remained completely slack throughout the trial were counted as successful autonomous walks.

sections.heading: Hardware Constraints and Previous Approaches to Locomotion
sections.summary: This section reviews Poppy's hardware specifications and prior work in bipedal locomotion, LQR, and system identification. The system operates in an asymmetric control loop where position command rates are capped at roughly 5 Hz, whereas joint angles can be read at around 100 Hz.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Poppy Humanoid Specifications
Poppy stands about 83 cm tall, weighs approximately 3.5 kg, houses an Odroid XU4 running Ubuntu Linux in its head with an RGB camera, and is actuated by 25 Dynamixel servomotors. Commands and state readings run through PyPot, a Python API; torque control is not supported. While modern humanoid controllers typically rely on high-frequency torque control above 100 Hz, Poppy exhibits jerky, unstable behavior when target positions are sent faster than 5 Hz. Conversely, joint angle feedback can be sampled reliably at around 100 Hz. This creates a unique setup: roughly 20 sensor readings are recorded between consecutive 5 Hz command updates.

### 2.2 Bipedal Locomotion Methods
Bipedal walking requires handling underactuation and dynamic discontinuities from contact transitions. Classic approaches include Zero Moment Point (ZMP) trajectory generation, trajectory optimization, and finite-state machines (FSMs) for stance/swing phase transitions. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) and sim-to-real transfer have achieved remarkable walking results, though they generally assume accurate simulation models and rich sensor feedback.

### 2.3 & 2.4 LQR and System Identification
LQR is an optimal feedback control method that minimizes quadratic cost functions for linear systems. For nonlinear robots, time-varying linearizations along a trajectory (TV-LQR) have been widely adopted. Meanwhile, system identification (SI) from real-world data has evolved from traditional physical parameter estimation into modern techniques that bridge the sim-to-real gap. This study builds on this foundation using local linear system identification coupled with LQR.

sections.heading: Formulating a 'Fall-Preventing Cost Function' via Convex Optimization
sections.summary: Using joint data from 125 open-loop walking trials, the authors identified local linear dynamics matrices via least squares. They then solved a semidefinite program (SDP) designed to penalize trials that end in falls, yielding an optimal LQR cost function.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Nominal Trajectory Design
Initial attempts with inverse kinematics and simulation-based dynamic trajectory optimization were either too slow or failed to transfer to hardware. Therefore, the authors started from a trajectory generated in physical simulation and refined target angles and timings through trial and error on the real robot. The final trajectory comprises two steps per cycle (left and right). Swing phases receive commands at roughly 5 Hz (the maximum reliable rate), followed by a 1.25-second dwell time after double support to let the motors settle.

### 3.2 Trajectory Playback Adjustments
Tracking accuracy was boosted by doubling the built-in PID proportional gain (P-gain) from 4 to 8. However, this caused the robot to reach waypoints too early. To fix this, target positions were intentionally set further ahead while applying a strict velocity limit, ensuring the robot reached target configurations exactly at the scheduled time.

### 3.3 Open-Loop Data Collection
The team ran 125 open-loop walking trials (6 steps per trial) across three locations. To observe dynamics around the nominal trajectory, Gaussian noise with standard deviation $\sigma \in \{0.0^\circ, 0.125^\circ, 0.25^\circ\}$ was added to waypoint targets. Recording the number of successful steps revealed that falls occurred even without added noise, showing that joint tracking errors gradually compound over time.

### 3.4 Residual Tracking via LQR
Variable-length observations (about 20 samples) between successive control commands (approx. 0.2 s) were linearly interpolated to $\overline{M}$ evenly spaced points, yielding a fixed-length state vector $x_n \in \mathbb{R}^{25 \cdot \overline{M}}$. For deviations $\delta x_n, \delta u_n$ relative to the nominal trajectory, time-varying linear dynamics $\delta x_{n+1} = A_n \delta x_n + B_n \delta u_n$ and quadratic costs were defined to derive optimal feedback gains $K_n$.

### 3.5 Linear System Identification
Residual data at each waypoint was used to fit the matrices $[A_n, B_n]$ via least-squares regression. While increasing $\overline{M}$ pushed prediction error below $0.1^\circ$, it also caused condition numbers to spike, inducing numerical instability. Hence, $\overline{M}=2$ was selected.

### 3.6 Learning a Cost Function to Prevent Falls
This is the core contribution of the paper. Defining the cost matrix as $C_n = \begin{bmatrix} Q_n & S_n \\ S_n^T & R_n \end{bmatrix}$, the authors formulated the following convex optimization problem:

- Objective: Keep $C_n$ as close to the identity matrix $I$ as possible (preventing the robot from straying far from nominal motion or adopting degenerative safe-stop behaviors)
- Inequality constraints: Ensure the average cost per unit time for falling trials exceeds that of successful trials by at least a margin $\epsilon$
- Positive semidefinite constraints: Enforce $C_n \succeq 0$ to satisfy LQR requirements

This yields a semidefinite program (SDP) whose global optimum can be solved efficiently with CVXPY. The optimization naturally resolves temporal credit assignment across waypoints to isolate which phases triggered the falls.

captions.F3: Histograms showing the number of successful steps before falling in open-loop trials. The left plot shows unperturbed runs ($\sigma=0.0$), and the right shows all data. Even with identical command inputs and no added noise, cumulative errors eventually cause the robot to fall.

sections.heading: Rigorous Evaluation Across 360 Trials: Closed-Loop Control Significantly Boosts Walking Success
sections.summary: Stability analysis on the margin parameter $\epsilon$ led to selecting $\epsilon=-2$ for closed-loop stability. Testing against open-loop playback in an office (100 trials each) and an unseen lab environment (80 trials each) confirmed statistically significant gains in walking performance.
sections.details:
### 4.1 LQR Stability Analysis
The authors evaluated the spectral radius $\lambda^*_n$ of the closed-loop matrix $A_n + B_n K_n$. If the cumulative product $\Lambda_n = \prod \lambda^*$ across a full cycle remains below 1, the system is stable. A margin of $\epsilon=0$ (strictly separating falling and successful trials) produced an unstable controller. Analyzing eigenvalues showed that overly strict constraints introduced zero eigenvalues into $C_n$, flattening the cost function in certain directions and leaving LQR unable to suppress errors along those modes. Relaxing the constraint with $\epsilon=-2$ to tolerate minor violations eliminated this singularity, producing a stable controller.

### 4.2 Walking Performance Comparison on Real Hardware
The closed-loop LQR controller was benchmarked against baseline open-loop playback in an extensive trial series. To prevent motor overheating, tests alternated conditions every 20 trials with rest breaks of at least 5 minutes. Since the step-count data is ordinal and non-normally distributed, comparisons were evaluated using Mann-Whitney $U$ tests.

- Office environment (carpeted floor, same room as training data, 100 trials each):
  - Open-loop: 62% success rate (mean 4.18 steps before falling)
  - Closed-loop: 78% success rate (mean 5.13 steps before falling)
  - $p$-value: 0.00225 (statistically significant improvement)

- Lab environment (slick, polished floor, unseen during training, 80 trials each):
  - Open-loop: 30% success rate (mean 3.75 steps before falling)
  - Closed-loop: 42.5% success rate (mean 4.80 steps before falling)
  - $p$-value: 0.00014 (statistically significant improvement)

Although performance dropped overall on the slippery lab floor, closed-loop control maintained a clear edge over open-loop, confirming its ability to generalize to novel surfaces.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: A New Starting Point for Low-Spec Humanoid Locomotion
sections.summary: This study demonstrated improved walking performance on an inexpensive, sensor-sparse Poppy humanoid through data-driven closed-loop LQR. Future directions include advanced system identification and leveraging untapped telemetry and RGB camera data to optimize walking speed and Cost of Transport (CoT).
sections.details:
This work represents a key initial step toward reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on the off-the-shelf standard Poppy Humanoid. By identifying local linear dynamics from open-loop data and learning fall-avoiding quadratic costs via convex optimization, the researchers achieved statistically significant gains in walking reliability on real hardware.

Future work highlights several promising directions:
- Applying more sophisticated system identification techniques to improve model accuracy
- Integrating currently unused sensor streams, such as motor temperature, load readings, and head-mounted RGB camera video
- Optimizing task-level walking performance metrics, including forward velocity, turning radius, and Cost of Transport (CoT), rather than purely preventing falls

Estimating body states via camera optical flow and combining that with velocity-conditioned reinforcement learning or control-theoretic methods could lead to even more versatile locomotion skills.

takeaways: Even under crippling hardware constraints—5 Hz command rate, position control only, 1-DOF ankles, and no IMU—closed-loop walking can be achieved using data-driven local linearization and LQR

Designing LQR cost functions that separate fall and success trajectories can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP), solving globally and uniquely via convex optimization without manual heuristics

Overly strict margin constraints can render the cost matrix singular (introducing zero eigenvalues) and destabilize unpenalized directions; relaxing constraints ($\epsilon < 0$) is crucial for closed-loop stability
For budget robots where sim-to-real transfer is tough, using the robot's own open-loop failure history as training data proves to be a highly practical strategy
limitations: Fall labels are assigned at step-level granularity, meaning the exact moment a fall becomes irreversible (the point of no return) is not precisely pinpointed
The controller is limited to tracking a single hand-tuned walking pattern and cannot adjust walking speed, turn, or navigate uneven terrain
Dynamics identification relies on simple linear least squares without mechanisms to adapt online to changing floor friction or mechanical wear and tear over time
